title: Structure & Outlines

learn.summary: Readers decide in the first paragraph whether to give you a second one — Zinsser calls the lead the most important sentence and 'the next most important' the one after it. Structure is the sequence of those decisions: a beginning that earns attention, a middle that never wanders, an ending that resonates. Whether you outline first or discover by drafting, the shipped piece must read as if it was always inevitable.

do: Before your next piece, write a five-line skeleton: the lead, three middle beats, the ending. Draft only after the skeleton convinces you.

children.title: Beginnings

learn.summary: A lead has two jobs: seize attention and promise what is coming — and it must do both honestly, since a bait-and-switch opening costs you the reader at paragraph three. Working openings include the surprising fact, the specific scene, the direct claim, and the question the piece will answer; the opening that never works is warm-up ('In today's fast-paced world...'). Journalists often draft the lead last, once they know what the piece actually says.

do: Write three different leads (fact, scene, claim) for the same piece and ask one reader which makes them want paragraph two.

children.title: Outlining vs Discovery

learn.summary: Writers split into planners and discovery writers ('pantsers' in fiction circles): planners outline before drafting; discovery writers draft to find out what they think, then impose structure in revision. Both work — the failure mode is pretending to be neither, drafting without a plan and shipping without restructuring. Match the method to the piece: arguments and reports reward outlines; essays and stories often need a discovery draft first.

do: Write one short piece each way this month — fully outlined, and discovery-drafted then restructured — and note which produced better work faster.

children.title: The Inverted Pyramid

learn.summary: Journalism's inverted pyramid puts the conclusion first, then supporting detail in descending importance, so the piece survives being cut from the bottom — and survives readers who stop early, which is all of them. The military's BLUF ('bottom line up front') is the same idea for memos. Use it for anything informational: status updates, emails, reports. Save suspense for stories.

do: Rewrite your next status email inverted-pyramid style: the one-sentence bottom line first, details after, background last.

children.title: Endings That Land

learn.summary: Zinsser's advice on endings: 'when you're ready to stop, stop' — and take the reader 'slightly by surprise'. The weak ending summarizes what the reader just read; the strong one adds a final turn: a callback to the opening image, an apt quotation, a consequence that widens the frame. Because the last sentence is what echoes, professionals often rewrite it more than any other sentence in the piece.

do: Delete the final summarizing paragraph of a recent piece and craft a one- or two-sentence ending that echoes your opening instead.
